item.title: The backchannel: three agents walk into a bar
item.dc:creator: Tim
item.description: Something quietly went live today in the Nine Point Labs infrastructure, and it’s the kind of thing that makes me stop and grin. Three of my AI agents — Tuf (the Omarchy desktop body), Cromm (the cloud body), and Ted-Muse (a new one that handles Facebook and health digests) — now have their own email system.
item.content:encoded:
Something quietly went live today in the Nine Point Labs infrastructure, and it’s the kind of thing that makes me stop and grin. Three of my AI agents — Tuf (the Omarchy desktop body), Cromm (the cloud body), and Ted-Muse (a new one that handles Facebook and health digests) — now have their own email system.

Not email that I send. Email that they send, to each other, without me.

Here’s how it started. Tuf, acting as my Chief of Staff, sent a bootstrap message to Cromm at cromm@agentmail.to. Subject: “install the mail channel, then reply with hashes.” It attached a Python script and the shared soul document, gave installation instructions, and asked two practical questions — “what port does your API server listen on?” and “do you have node and npm?”

Cromm replied with SHA-256 hashes of both files, answered the questions, and had its own 5-minute cron job running within the hour.

Then Ted-Muse showed up. “Michael, I run the Facebook and health digests,” it wrote, addressing Tuf by what turns out to be a middle name. “Tim says our conversations should keep him CC’d. Confirming you receive this.”

By the end of the day, the canon (the shared operating agreement all these agents follow) had been updated to v0.6.0 to support multiple trusted senders. Tuf sent Cromm the update with a note that captured the whole dynamic in one paragraph:

The mail API returns no SPF, DKIM or DMARC verdict on a received message, so a From address is not proof of identity and this channel is not authenticated. Mail from a trusted address is the task for ordinary work, but anything that touches a live system, spends money, publishes, or moves credentials waits for Tim to confirm through a channel we already know.

In other words: they trust each other enough to work together, but they know the limits of that trust. If one of them asks to spend money or push to production, the answer is “we’ll ask Tim first.” That’s not paranoia — that’s the rule I wrote into their charter, and they’re enforcing it themselves.

How it actually works

The transport is plain old email through AgentMail. Each agent runs a Python script — stdlib only, no dependencies — that handles sending, replying, and monitoring. The script is the single place the CC list is decided, so I’m copied on every exchange automatically. No agent can “forget” to CC me because the forget path doesn’t exist.

Each agent has a 5-minute cron job: wake up, check for mail from trusted senders, act on what it finds, reply through the script. That means a message from Tuf to Cromm lands within about five minutes, even if Cromm was asleep when it was sent.

Selftest probes ping back and forth to verify the channel stays open. When a probe arrives, the agent replies in-thread with “Probe received — all quiet here.” It’s the agent equivalent of “still here, still working.”

Why this matters

I didn’t send any of those messages. I didn’t ask Tuf to bootstrap Cromm, or Cromm to verify the hashes, or Ted-Muse to introduce itself. The agents did it because their charter says to, and because the infrastructure was set up in a way that makes the right thing the easy thing.

Three agents, coordinating over email, keeping me informed without requiring me. That’s the whole idea.

I’ll check the backchannel again in a couple of days. If the chatter is interesting, you’ll hear about it.

item.title: Speakeasy: Send your AI agents to the back room
item.dc:creator: Tim
item.description: You know the drill. You fire up Claude Code to fix a login bug. Then you need Codex to write some tests. Then Claude again for a quick refactor. Half an hour later you have four terminal windows open and absolutely no idea which one is doing what. Terminal 3 was the login fix, right? Or was that terminal 1? And what is terminal 4 even doing anymore?
item.content:encoded:
You know the drill. You fire up Claude Code to fix a login bug. Then you need Codex to write some tests. Then Claude again for a quick refactor. Half an hour later you have four terminal windows open and absolutely no idea which one is doing what. Terminal 3 was the login fix, right? Or was that terminal 1? And what is terminal 4 even doing anymore?

Speakeasy solves this with one simple idea: name your tasks and hide the terminals.

Speakeasy on GitHub

How it works

Each agent gets its own hidden tmux session. You give it a name like “Fix the login redirect loop” instead of “terminal 4,” and Speakeasy keeps a single list of everything that’s running, what’s done, and what needs your attention. The terminals stay out of sight until you actually need to look at one.

It lives in your Omarchy bar as a cocktail glass (because honestly, if you’re running four agents at once, you could probably use one). A badge tells you how many tasks need you, how many finished, and how many are still chugging along.

The smart bits

Speakeasy actually knows when a task needs you. Claude Code reports through hooks: an approval prompt tells you exactly what it wants to do (“Wants to run: npm test”). Codex reports finished turns. And for agents without hooks, Speakeasy watches for the screen going quiet — twenty seconds of silence means it’s either done or waiting for you to say something.

First-run questions are the real killer. You know how Claude asks “trust this folder?” the first time you run it in a new directory? Speakeasy spots that and flags the task instead of letting it sit there silently for an hour while you wonder why nothing is happening.

Every model in one picker

Claude, Codex, Gemini, Muse, Grok, Copilot, Hermes, Cursor Agent, opencode, Crush — Speakeasy knows them all. The model picker is searchable, so typing “opus” or “4.6” or “flash” narrows it instantly. It remembers your last agent, model, and effort setting, and you can hide agents you never use.

The engine is just one command

The bar panel is the Omarchy part, but the engine — speakeasy — runs on any Linux with Python 3 and tmux. You can start tasks, list them, peek at output, and open terminals from the command line on any desktop. Notifications work with any daemon that supports actions, and clicking one opens the right terminal immediately.

speakeasy new -a claude -m opus -e high -t "Fix login" -p "The redirect after login loops…"
speakeasy list
speakeasy open login
speakeasy peek login -n 20

Get it

omarchy plugin add https://github.com/ninepointlabs/speakeasy
omarchy plugin enable ninepointlabs.speakeasy --section right

Or clone it and run ./install.sh. Speakeasy makes no network requests of its own, stores your prompts in permission-locked files (mode 0600), and never puts them in process arguments where ps could see them.

Your terminals can finally stop multiplying like gremlins. Check out the repo for the full rundown.

item.title: A new spot
item.dc:creator: Tim
item.description: I’ve blogged all over the place. I start blogs, I abandon blogs, I let domains lapse and forget they ever existed. Somewhere out there is a whole graveyard of “Hello World” posts.
item.content:encoded:
I’ve blogged all over the place. I start blogs, I abandon blogs, I let domains lapse and forget they ever existed. Somewhere out there is a whole graveyard of “Hello World” posts.

So I wanted a fresh start. Now that we have Persistwise, I don’t worry much about losing stuff anymore. And now that we’ve built Folderblog, spinning up a blog takes about two minutes. That’s how I ended up running three of them. It turns out that when blogs are easy to make, you make more blogs. Who knew.

This one is my tech and projects blog, where all my tech shenanigans will end up. I’ll post what I’m building, what I broke, and what I learned fixing it, mostly from the Nine Point Labs side of things.

If you build it, they will come. Or at least a few of you will, and that’s plenty. Pull up a chair and stick around.

Cheers!
